chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated to us, he said: Al-Qasim ibn Ali narrated to us from Abi Basir from Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

My father struck his servant boy with a single whip. He had sent him on an errand but he delayed [in doing what was required]. So the servant boy cried and said, 'Allah! O Ali ibn al-Husayn, you send me on an errand and then strike me?!' So my father began to cry and said [to me], 'O my son, go to the grave of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and offer two rak'ahs of prayer, and then say, "O Allah, forgive Ali ibn al-Husayn for his mistake on the Day of Judgment."' Then he told the servant boy, 'Go, for you are free in the way of Allah!' Abi Basir said, 'I asked him, "May I be your ransom! Was the emancipation [of his servant] an expiation for the sin?' But he remained silent.
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the Imam's silence regarding whether emancipation is an expiation for striking a servant?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Kitab al-Zuhd* highlights the spiritual sensitivity of Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin) to minor sins, illustrating the Shia emphasis on *adab* (etiquette) and mercy within the household. The Imam’s silence upon being asked if emancipation was the specific *kaffarah* for striking indicates that while freeing the slave was a meritorious act of atonement, it was not necessarily the exclusive or legally mandated expiation, distinguishing between voluntary piety and fixed jurisprudence. This incident underscores the Prophet's family's practice of linking personal accountability directly to the intercession of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his progeny).
